                        Norway's sovereign wealth fund, the world's largest with assets of more than $2 trillion, on Thursday reported a negative return of 278 billion kroner ($31 billion) in the third quarter as it was weighed down by higher interest rates.

It posted a negative return of 0.5 percent in the quarter, dragged down by a negative return of 3.5 percent in its fixed-income investments, while its equity and property portfolios increased by 0.5 percent and 0.4 percent respectively.

"The fund's return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments," the fund's deputy CEO Trond Grande said in a statement.

Invested primarily in equities, bonds and real estate across the globe, the fund reported a value of 22,014 billion kroner at the end of September.

Inflation around the world, fuelled in particular by soaring energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East, has led several central banks, including the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, to raise interest rates in the third quarter.

"Equity returns were also close to zero, but there were large differences between sectors. Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell," Grande said.

Fuelled by the Nordic country's oil revenues, the fund is invested in more than 7,100 companies spanning the globe, and holds around 1.5 percent of all listed companies worldwide, making it the world's largest single investor.

articles.title: IN DATA: Who were the 5,000 foreigners deported from Norway last year?
articles.content:

Photo by Blake Guidry on Unsplash

                        As well as tracking how many people move to Norway, the Directorate of Immigration (UDI) also monitors foreign nationals ordered to leave the country (with British citizens throwing up a surprise).

In 2025, Norwegian authorities issued formal deportation orders (utvisningsvedtak) to 5,002 foreign nationals, according to statistics from UDI.

A deportation order in Norway carries a formal entry ban, which prevents the person from returning to Norway for a certain period, or permanently in serious cases. It can even include a ban from entering the Schengen Area.

One of the main reasons a foreign resident can be deported from Norway is breaking the Immigration Act. This includes administrative violations like overstaying a visa, working without a valid permit, giving false information on residency applications, or not leaving the country after an asylum or visa refusal.

In 2025, 4,125 orders (which represents 82.5 percent of the total deportation orders) were issued on these grounds.

Foreign nationals can also be expelled from Norway after a criminal conviction, but this is much less common. Last year there were 368 such cases (7.4 percent of all deportation orders).

Contrary to popular belief, EU citizens are not exempt from being expelled from Norway, even though they have freedom of movement under the EEA Agreement.

In 2025, 500 orders (10 percent of all cases) were issued to European nationals. This can happen on grounds such as public order, public security, or abuse of rights.

In 2025, most deportation orders were given to nationals from South Asia and West Africa.

India had the highest number of cases with 949 in total. Of these, 941 were for immigration breaches and eight for criminal convictions. Pakistan was next with 918 orders, 917 for immigration breaches and one for a criminal conviction.

There was then a sharp drop. Bangladesh came third with 331 orders (329 for immigration breaches and two for criminal offences), and Nigeria in fourth place with 227 orders (218 for immigration breaches and nine for criminal convictions).

Combined, nationals from these four countries made up nearly 49 percent of all deportation orders in Norway in 2025.

Further down the overall list among non-EEA states were countries like Kenya with 112, Nepal (139), Ghana (111), China (78), the UK (62), Ukraine (59), and the United States with 42.

Australia and Canada recorded just 8 and 10 orders, respectively.

Among the European nationals, the highest number of expulsion orders was issued to citizens from Romania (160), Lithuania (89), Poland (75), and neighbouring Sweden (64), followed by the Netherlands (20), Latvia (13), and Spain (12).

UK nationals top list of convicted criminals deported

The figures show an unexpected trend in criminal deportations. Of the 62 British citizens ordered to leave in 2025, 35 were deported after criminal convictions. This made the UK the country with the most convicted criminals deported from Norway last year, ahead of Ukraine (33), China (31), and the United States (19).

A further 25 Britons were expelled for immigration status violations after losing EU freedom of movement post-Brexit.

READ ALSO: Indians, Brits and Syrians top Norway's permanent residency list

UDI statistics show a steady increase in expulsions in recent years.

Norwegian authorities recorded 1,210 deportation orders in 2021, 1,894 in 2022, 2,893 in 2023, and 3,302 in 2024. With the total passing the 5,000 mark in 2025, expulsion orders were more than four times higher than four years prior.

articles.content:

                        Norway expects almost 2,000 fewer refugees next year, details from the Storting gala dinner and King Haakon's speech, and more news on Friday.

Almost 2,000 fewer refugees expected in Norway next year

This marks the lowest expected number since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Norwegian municipalities have resettled over 110,000 refugees, most of whom came from Ukraine.

"There has been a marked decline in recent years, but from a historically high level. The number to be resettled next year is still significant in a Norwegian context," said Libe Rieber-Mohn, director of IMDi.​

Minister of Labour and Social Inclusion Kjersti Stenseng also explained in a statement: "The Labour Party government has taken a number of steps to limit the number of displaced people coming to Norway. We are now seeing the results of that. We will not accept more than we can integrate, while continuing to stand up for Ukraine and ensure a safe stay for displaced people in Norway."

The ministry said that several municipalities are experiencing pressure on housing markets and local public services (such as schools, kindergartens, and health and care facilities) following several years of high settlement numbers. Authorities also pointed out that secondary migration is an issue, as refugees sometimes move away from the municipality where they first settled.

​In response, officials are introducing tighter criteria for resettlement requests next year, which they say will help with integration and prevent segregation.

"The government has changed the criteria for requests to avoid settling refugees in areas with big challenges and to make it easier to find work quickly. Because of this, municipalities like Fredrikstad, Sarpsborg, and Halden will not be asked to settle refugees in 2027," Stenseng said.

Daily smoking falls in Norway, especially among Gen Z

In its latest survey on tobacco, alcohol, and substance use, Statistics Norway (SSB) reported that daily cigarette smoking has dropped to 6 percent, down from 7 percent last year. Meanwhile, daily use of snus, the small nicotine pouches, remains more than twice as common at 15 percent, reaching 22 percent among men.

"Over the past 10 years, there have been changes in the population's tobacco habits, and there are now more than twice as many daily users of snus compared to daily smokers," said Sindre Mikael Haugen, a senior adviser at Statistics Norway, in an accompanying article.

The agency also pointed out a clear generational divide in tobacco use as generation Z could be Norway’s first generation with very few daily smokers.

"To use a widely used generational division, one could say that Gen Z (1997–2012) is possibly the first generation without, and Millennials (1981–1996) the last generation with, a significant proportion of people who have smoked daily," Haugen said.

Interestingly, the figures also show that very few people both smoke and use snus every day. This suggests the two habits rarely happen together.

​King Haakon and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra mark historic "firsts" at Storting gala dinner

On Thursday evening, the Royal Palace in Oslo held one of Norway’s most prestigious and high-profile traditions (established in 1906): the annual parliamentary dinner (Stortingsmiddagen), where the monarch invites the 169 members of the Storting, cabinet ministers, and other senior state officials to the Palace.

The evening was a significant milestone for the royal family, as King Haakon hosted the gala for the first time as monarch, while Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra wore her first formal gala dress as Crown Princess.

The King’s speech is always a highlight, mixing thoughts about the nation with a personal touch. King Haakon started his speech by honouring his father, the late King Harald, in a very personal way: "So it's me standing here, not my father. I miss him tonight, and I'm sure I'm not alone. This was his arena. He was, as we know, funny—with apt comments and good timing. And not infrequently, dad jokes."

The King made the audience laugh when he talked about how long he had prepared for the role: "As you probably understand, it's not easy to become king overnight. Then having 35 years of experience as a middle manager in a medium-sized public enterprise comes in handy."

He also thanked Queen Mette-Marit for her support: "And it's important to have good people around you—and I'm lucky in that, because I have the Queen on my team. It gives me security and support."

Looking ahead, the King said: "I've had a fantastic coach in any case. Now it's just a matter of managing my energy well. This is a long-distance race, and I'm aiming for consistent speed and good endurance."

Jens Elmelund Kjeldsen, a professor of rhetoric at the University of Bergen, told newspaper Aftenposten the speech was full of metaphors and called it "a factual defence of constitutional democracy."

If you are curious about what the monarch and politicians ate at such a prestigious national gala, public broadcaster NRK shared the details. Guests were served a four-course menu consisting of crab salad, cheese tart, moose from Sikkilsdalen (hunted by the late King Harald's hunting party), and traditional Norwegian cloudberries for dessert.

Norwegian vocabulary: Stortingsmiddagen - the parliamentary dinner

​Practice grenade found in luggage at Tromsø Airport

Police were called to Tromsø Airport on Thursday afternoon after a grenade was discovered in checked baggage during a routine security screening.

Authorities later said there was no danger to the public as the item was a training grenade, not a real one.

"We need to be completely certain before handling it further, which is why our specialists are assessing it," police told public broadcaster NRK before the item was formally cleared.

The security alert caused some delays at the airport, but things soon returned to normal.

articles.title: T-banen i Oslo stenger i fire dager i november
articles.content:
63 av 101 T-banestasjoner i Oslo stenges i fire dager fra 19. november. Årsaken er at Sporveien skal teste nytt signalsystem og deretter bytte tilbake.

Fra torsdag 19. november til og med søndag 22. november vil det ikke gå T-bane gjennom Oslo sentrum. 63 av 101 stasjoner blir stengt, inkludert alle stasjonene i sentrum.

– Det får konsekvenser for hele kollektivtilbudet, skriver Ruter i en pressemelding.

Det vil bli satt opp et tilbud under stengingen, men Ruter opplyser at det ikke er mulig å erstatte T-banen med ekstra busser eller trikker.

Stengingen er den første av sju – som fortsetter i 2027. Neste gang blir fra 25. til 28. februar neste år.

articles.title: WSJ: Trump skal ha ringt Musk og bedt ham oppheve Starlink-begrensning
articles.content:
De ikke navngitte kildene sier til Wall Street Journal torsdag at systemet tilsynelatende fungerer mer som normalt kort tid etter samtalen torsdag.

articles.content:

                        The healthcare sector in Norway is facing staffing shortages, with future forecasts looking even more worrying. New data now shows how important immigrant workers are for the system (despite strict authorisation requirements.)

Over the past ten years, more immigrants have started working in Norway’s health and care services, according to new figures from Statistics Norway (SSB).

In 2025, nearly 88,000 immigrants worked in health and care services, up from 56,000 in 2015. Including foreign commuters, international workers now account for 19.5 percent of all staff in the sector, a rise of 5.1 percentage points over ten years.

This means that roughly one in five people employed in healthcare in Norway is an immigrant.

The upward trend shows that Norway is relying more on international staff. With ongoing shortages in the health service, where many residents still struggle even to secure an assigned GP, foreign workers are helping to ease the blow.

Around 90 percent of the growth in immigrant employment over the past ten years has been in direct patient care roles, where immigrants now account for 20.1 percent of the workforce. This amounts to an increase of 31,600 people in ten years.

For example, among healthcare assistants (helsefagarbeidere), more than one in four workers (27.3 percent) is an immigrant. Regarding this role, SSB said that without foreign workers, the number of healthcare assistants in Norway would have dropped by more than 10 percent over the past decade, instead of increasing by 2 percent.

Immigrants also make up 23.2 percent of doctors and 15.3 percent of registered nurses in the country.

However, growth among nurses has been slower, with the SSB attributing the trend to stricter requirements for healthcare personnel with foreign education when seeking Norwegian professional authorisation.

Many of these employees have lived in Norway for a long time, as out of the 88,000 foreign-born staff, 31 percent have been in the country for over 20 years.

Most moved for reasons other than work, and only 25 percent said they came for a job or have a Nordic background.

When looking at where foreign healthcare workers are employed, the highest concentration is in Oslo and Akershus. In these areas, more than one in three healthcare staff members is an immigrant.

Nevertheless, rural districts also rely on them just as heavily. In rural and remote parts of Norway, foreign-born staff make up almost 18 percent of health workers.

The figures above show personnel directly employed in Norway’s healthcare services, but the system also depends a lot on temporary staffing agencies.

These agencies provide staff from third-party firms to work in Norwegian hospitals and municipal care services, mainly hiring doctors, nurses, and healthcare assistants.

Across these positions, immigrants make up the vast majority of the workforce. For instance, among temporary agency nurses, 79 percent are immigrants or foreign commuters, with Spain representing the single largest country of origin, followed by Lithuania and Sweden.

Regarding doctors working for these agencies, the majority come from Sweden.

Long-term official projections estimate that Norway will face a national deficit of roughly 42,400 full-time equivalents across core healthcare roles by 2040.

With Norway recording its lowest labour immigration in 20 years in 2025, SSB said that any sustained slowdown in foreign recruitment would widen this deficit: "If it turns out that immigration is lower, it will contribute to the gap between supply and demand being larger than projected."

However, a Healthcare Personnel Commission appointed by the government has warned against relying on international staff. They argued that foreign workers require extensive language training to work effectively with patients and that international staff are often less stable, since many return home or move to other countries after some time in Norway.

The Ministry of Labour and Social Inclusion have shared these concerns and said that depending too much on foreign labour makes Norway’s key public services more vulnerable during international crises or war.

                        Norway's immigration appeals board trials AI for case summaries, ​Oslo's new district names given the green light, don't trust anyone asking you to buy gold, and more news this Thursday.

Norway's immigration appeals board trials AI for case summaries

Norway's Immigration Appeals Board (UNE), which handles appeals in immigration cases following decisions by the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI), has started using artificial intelligence to draft summaries for some specific types of cases.

According to the newspaper Utrop, the summaries are published in UNE's public legal database, where lawyers and legal representatives consult to examine how the board has ruled on similar asylum and immigration cases in the past.

The agency emphasised that AI does not make any actual decisions on residence applications, that two human caseworkers review every text before publication, and that they pay strict attention to privacy, as each case can contain sensitive information.

One in ten property ads in Norway misleads on bedroom numbers

A new inspection by the Norwegian Consumer Authority (Forbrukertilsynet) across ten of Norway's largest estate agency chains found that 10 percent of marketed homes falsely advertised having more bedrooms than they actually do.

The authority found that agencies often list bedrooms based on how rooms are used and not on what they are approved for, as some rooms are not authorised for permanent residence, and others have not even been built yet.

"The survey shows that the real estate industry has room for clearer and less misleading information in the marketing of bedrooms. Consumers must be able to trust that the information they receive is correct," said Bente Øverli, director at the Norwegian Consumer Authority.

Among the agencies investigated were Aktiv Eiendomsmegling, DNB Eiendom, Eie Franchise, Eiendomsmegler 1, Eiendomsmegler Norge, Krogsveen Eiendom, Nordvik Bolig, Privatmegleren, Proaktiv Gruppen, and &Partner.

Norwegian vocabulary: boligannonser  - housing advertising

The Local has covered this story on several occasions throughout what has been a lengthy process, but on Wednesday, the City Council formally adopted the names of what will become Oslo's eight new districts from January 1st, 2028.

"I am pleased that we have put in place the names for what will become Oslo's eight districts. Now we can also start referring to the new districts by name. Even though most of us probably feel the strongest sense of belonging to the place where we live, whether it is Røa or Vålerenga, I hope the new names will be experienced as unifying for the residents of the new districts," said Health and Districts Councillor Oluf Ulseth in a press release.

On September 24th, the City Council presented its final recommendation for the names, which sparked a debate on the matter.

According to public broadcaster NRK, the approval faced resistance from several parties who suggested changing some of the names, but without success. The Green Party (MDG) and the Red Party even suggested using numbers instead of names for the new districts.

At the same time, the County Governor will look into whether the decision might be illegal after a request from the Red party which argues that making such a big change without a proper investigation is unlawful.

The final names are: Vestre Aker, Gamle Aker, Gamle Oslo, Frysja, Hovin, Øvre Groruddalen, Østensjø, and Nordstrand.

Oslo residents will already see the new names during the municipal elections in September 2027, when they vote for representatives to the new district committees.

Norwegian banks warn of bizarre scam asking victims to leave gold in forests

Banking industry organisation Finance Norway (Finans Norge) has issued an alert over several new fraud methods targeting both individuals and businesses in Norway.

These include a bizarre gold investment scam where victims are tricked into buying large amounts of gold and leaving it in outdoor places, like forests, for fraudsters to pick up later.

"Be very sceptical if someone contacts you and asks you to invest in gold or other valuables. Do not hand over valuables to strangers or leave them in places following instructions from others," said Gry Nergård, director of anti-fraud at Finans Norge, in a press release.

The organisation also warned against fraudulent messages impersonating cosmetics retailer Lyko, where recipients are told they have won a prize or a gift and prompted to click a malicious link to "verify" it, handing over sensitive information in the process.

Employees with access to company bank accounts were also urged to be careful. This scam usually starts with an SMS or email sent to a staff member, followed by a phone call where fraudsters pretend to be from for example, the company's bank or another trusted organisation.

According to Finans Norge, banks and consumers in Norway lost 962 million kroner to fraudulent schemes in 2025 alone.

                        Those living in Oslo have long perceived the city's distinct residential divisions, and new academic research now provides data to back up those impressions.

A study by researchers at NOVA at Oslo Metropolitan University, published by forskning.no, investigated how families in the capital region choose where to live, revealing clear patterns.

Using data from over 20,000 family moves between 1993 and 2017, the study showed that despite city policies to encourage integration, families’ choices still lead to demographic divisions in Oslo.

​Specifically, Norwegian-born parents from all income and wealth levels avoid moving to neighbourhoods with high proportions of non-Western immigrants.

​Lead researcher Professor Lena Magnusson Turner said this trend is worrying. “Although policy facilitates people from different socio-economic classes living in the same neighbourhood, we see that the population chooses differently.”

​Turner explained that people also look for neighbours who are similar to themselves, while less affluent families actively avoid areas where they would feel financially inferior.

“When people move and have the opportunity to choose, they move to neighbourhoods where they find people who are like them. People don't seek out neighbourhoods where the inequalities are too great,” she said.

​The study also established that accumulated wealth influences neighbourhood selection far more than income, leading the most affluent households to cluster in specific areas.

​When looking at families with children, the study revealed that parents with daughters care more about the economic status of their neighbours than parents with sons. “We think it's about ideas parents have about protecting their girls to a greater extent, while assuming boys can handle themselves,” Turner added.

articles.content:
De åtte nye bydelsnavnene i Oslo er endelig vedtatt.

Bystyret gikk onsdag inn for å kalle bydelene Vestre Aker, Gamle Aker, Gamle Oslo, Frysja, Hovin, Øvre Groruddalen, Østensjø og Nordstrand.

Fremskrittspartiet ville gi ytterligere to bydeler det gamle Aker-navnet, og foreslo Nordre Aker i stedet for Frysja og Østre Aker i stedet for Øvre Groruddalen.

MDG Eivind Trædal mente at «Grønnsaker» kunne vært et navn i tråd med partiets politikk, men endte altså med å gå for bydel 1, bydel 2 og så videre.

Selve bydelsreformen ble vedtatt i juni. Den innebærer at antall bydeler blir kuttet fra 15 til åtte 1. januar 2028.

Statsforvalteren skal undersøke om dette vedtaket kan være ulovlig etter krav fra Rødt.

                        Some 44 members of the European Parliament from 15 different EU countries and six political groups have called on EU transport ministers to break the deadlock and get the plan to end the seasonal changing of the clocks moving again.

In the middle of the night on Saturday 24th, people across Europe will once again turn the clocks back by one hour, ending daylight saving time. This means that people will gain an hour of sleep – which they had lost when turning the clocks forward in March.

The practice was introduced to save energy following the 1970s oil crisis. Since 2001, an EU directive obliges EU member states to act at the same time, moving the clocks forward by one hour on the last Sunday of March and backward on the last Sunday of October, to avoid changing time on different dates, with complications for transport, communications and cross-border activities.

READ MORE: Whatever happened to the EU's plan to stop changing the clocks?

In 2018, the European Commission launched a public consultation asking people their views on abolishing time changes. Some 4.6 million people responded, the most successful EU consultation ever, and 84 percent agreed with the idea to scrap the changing of the clocks.

In September 2018 the Commission therefore proposed legislation to put an end on seasonal clock changes. This had to be approved by the European Parliament and by national governments represented at the EU Council.

The European Parliament in 2019 supported the proposal by a large majority. But EU governments failed to reach an agreement. Should summertime or wintertime become the norm? How to coordinate the change among neighbouring countries to avoid a patchwork of different time zones? And who would benefit the most?

Last year, Spain revived the discussion, backed by Poland and Finland, but other Member States remained unconvinced.

On Tuesday, a group of MEPs addressed a letter to the transport ministers of the 27 EU countries asking them to break the deadlock and “finally get the negotiations in the Council… moving again”.

The letter was spearheaded by German MEP Peter Liese.

He said the lack of an agreement among countries “is irresponsible and shows once again that problems which people across Europe are concerned about are often not caused by the European institutions, but by those responsible in the Member States.”

“For eight years, Member States have used the lack of an impact assessment as an excuse for failing to act on the proposal. I believe this argument is a pretext. Nevertheless, it is good that the new study is finally coming,” he added.

A study commissioned by the EU executive on the impact of abolishing seasonal clock changes should be completed by the end of the year.

Liese, who is a medical doctor, also noted that health effects of changing the clocks twice a year include “sleep disturbances, fatigue and difficulties concentrating”. Recent studies also questioned the extent of energy savings achieved with the practice.

“There is no sensible reason to disrupt the daily rhythm of millions of people twice a year. Those responsible must finally take action,” he argued.

“We recognise that any solution must be carefully coordinated between Member States, particularly to avoid unnecessary complications for transport, cross-border activities and the functioning of the internal market. However, we firmly believe that all these challenges can be overcome if there is sufficient political will and close coordination between Member States,” the letter states.

                        Norwegian Right-wing party attacks immigration policy, one in five healthcare workers in Norway are immigrants, and more news on Wednesday.

One in five people employed in healthcare in Norway are immigrants

Over the past ten years, more immigrants have started working in Norway’s healthcare services, according to new figures from Statistics Norway (SSB), which has helped a sector that faces major staff shortages.

In 2025, nearly 88,000 immigrants worked in healthcare services, up from 56,000 in 2015. Including foreign commuters, international workers now account for 19.5 percent of all staff in the sector, a rise of 5.1 percentage points over ten years.

Many of these workers have lived in Norway for a long time. Of the 88,000 foreign-born staff, 31 percent have been in Norway for over 20 years while the majority immigrated for reasons other than work, with just 25 percent citing employment as their reason for moving or holding a Nordic background.

The biggest increase is in front line jobs. About 90 percent of the growth in immigrant employment over the past ten years has been in direct patient care roles, where immigrants now account for 20.1 percent of the workforce. This amounts to an increase of 31,600 personnel in 10 years.

Immigrants now account for more than one in four healthcare assistants (helsefagarbeidere) in Norway, or 27.3 percent, alongside 23.2 percent of doctors and 15.3 percent of nurses.

However, growth among nurses has been slower, with the SSB attributing the trend to stricter requirements for healthcare personnel with foreign education when seeking Norwegian professional authorisation.

Norwegian vocabulary: sysselsatt / å være sysselsatt - employed / to be in employment

Right-wing party launches fresh attack on immigration

Progress Party (Frp) leader Sylvi Listhaug, during a speech at the party's national council, has called for more restrictions on Norwegian immigration policy, arguing that Norway has been far too liberal and needs stricter requirements, according to the newspaper Dagsavisen.

Listhaug declared that the party needed to discuss "what many still do not dare to talk about", outlining a hardline package of proposals. These include limiting the possibility of bringing family members to Norway, introducing stricter income requirements, and making it more difficult to obtain permanent residence and Norwegian citizenship.

She also wants to establish asylum reception centres in other countries, so that asylum seekers would have their applications processed outside Norway.

Listhaug insisted that the measures will also benefit immigrants as long as they work, respect the law and contribute to the Norwegian system.

However, she argued that the main risk from immigration is not financial, but, as she put it, "it is the import of a medieval culture and values that do not belong in Norway."

The Progress Party is currently an opposition party to the governing Labour Party, meaning these measures are only proposals and would need a majority in the Storting to become law.

As the multicultural media Utrop said: "For immigrants planning family reunification, permanent residence or Norwegian citizenship, the rules in force still apply. Listhaug's speech nevertheless shows the direction the Progress Party wants to take immigration policy in the years to come."

Norwegian vocabulary: innvandringspolitikk  - immigration policy

Government cracks down on illegal tourism operators in the north

The government is implementing a series of targeted measures to stop illegal operations, undeclared labour, and criminal networks active in the northern travel industry.

The intervention follows warnings from Norway’s economic crime agency, Økokrim, which explained that criminal networks are increasingly taking advantage of the region’s tourism boom to launder money, evade taxes, and facilitate illegal employment.

"We must not be naive. When we get this information on the table, we must take it very seriously. We have no room for cowboys in our industry," said Minister of Trade and Industry Cecilie Myrseth, as reported by public broadcaster NRK.

The biggest problem identified is rogue operators running their businesses entirely outside Norway and its regulations.

Økokrim explained that "services such as northern lights tourism are sold from countries such as Brazil, Germany, and China. Payments are made to companies organised outside Norway, while the service itself is performed here without any tax revenue being left behind. These are typical signs of money laundering and tax evasion."

To stop these operations, authorities are adding more police and creating a special economic crime unit in the Troms Police District. They also plan to tighten controls on investments, set up a corporate transparency register, and form a security task force.

Norwegian vocabulary: ulovligheter - illegal activities

Oslo hosts high stakes talks between Zelensky and US envoys

Oslo became the centre of international diplomacy on Tuesday as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky held high-level talks in the capital with US envoys, to draw a line under a bitter feud between Kyiv's leader and US President Donald Trump over the war with Russia.

Flanked by Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Zelensky said it was "important that we keep the conversation going."

The Oslo meeting followed furious diplomatic efforts in Washington, Kyiv and Western capitals to calm the situation.

After the Tuesday meetings, Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff, was scheduled to travel to Russia on Wednesday for talks with President Vladimir Putin in a bid to end the four-year war in Ukraine, but recent reports from public broadcaster NRK say he has already come back to Oslo to meet with Støre.

Norwegian vocabulary: spesialutsending - special envoy
